title: DRAFT — Oxford Companion eponym attributions, quote-verified batch
description:
UN-APPLIED DRAFT. Second pass over docs/evidence/eponyms/companion-verdicts.tsv, covering rows the first companion-attributions manifest did not take. Scope: verdict='entry', the catalogue row carries no attributed_to, and the evidence states a definite role.

IMPORTANT — the evidence file's `role` column is a triage judgement and is NOT always supported by the quoted entry. Every candidate was therefore re-tested against its own quote, and only rows whose quote attributes an ACTION to the named person are here. Two failure modes were found and excluded: (a) the entry names the person only as the opening's eponym and says nothing about what they did (9 rows, e.g. 'Kevitz Defence, 42 in the ENGLISH OPENING.'); (b) the entry credits a different person with the origination while the triage assigned 'originator' to the eponym (2 rows, e.g. From's Gambit, which the Companion says was 'first given by GRECO'). Those 11 are in the sidecar files beside this manifest, with the reason per row.

Quotes are verbatim, OCR artefacts included, matching the applied manifest's convention. Role vocabulary follows the catalogue's British-spelling agent nouns. Disputed attributions stay CLEAR with the rival recorded in historical_notes, following the precedent of A.Eng.Mik. Apply-ready PENDING Albert's explicit GO. Whitespace inside quotes is collapsed to single spaces and trimmed, which the manifest validator requires and the applied companion manifest already observes; the OCR's intra-number spacing is preserved as-is.

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Kieseritzky Gambit': "Kieseritzky Gambit. 1 1 5 1 in the KING ' S GAMBIT Accepted . In the 1 840s KIESERITZKY did much to popularize this l ine, which dates from POLERIO, 1 590, and was analysed by SAL v10, 1 604, and PHILI DOR, 1 749. White seeks to demonstrate that the defence of the gambit pawn by 3 . . . g5 weakens Black's king's-side pawn formation. This positional aim, suggested first by Philidor and later by Rt.:BIN- STEIN, contrasts with the combinativc ideas that normally attach to the ALLGAIER and MUZIO GAM BITS. Black's best replies are the BERLIN and PAUL SEN L>EFI NCES ( 1 1 60, 1 1 63)."

Black reserves the option of dcf ending his gambit pawn while avoiding the hazards of the KIESERITZKY and ALLGAIER GAMBITS. Compare HECKER DEFENCE, 1 1 74, which is, perhaps, a less commendable way to achieve the same object."

Martin Villemson ( 1 897- 1 933) of Parnu, Estonia, editor of the chess magazine Eesti Maleilm, played it in the first International Correspondence Tournament of the Deutsche Schachzeitung. He was a strong correspondence player and may well have inspired KERES to try that activity, in which they overlapped."

Pioneered by BIRD, e.g. against ANDERSSEN in 1 854, and used on occasion by grandmasters such as TARRASCH, SPASSKY, and MALANYUK, this defence has not gained wide acceptance."

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Zaitsev Variation'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Zaitsev Variation': "Zaitsev Variation, 543 in the SICILIAN DEFENCE; 772 in the SPANISH OPENING, recommended in 1 973 and 1 968 respectively by the Soviet player Igor Arkadyevich Zaitsev ( 1 938 - ). Sometimes used for the LENZERHEIDE VARIATION, 747."

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Morphy Defense to the Ruy Lopez'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Morphy Defense to the Ruy Lopez': "Morphy Defence. 674 in the SPANISH OPENING. This move, 3 . . . a6, first given by DEL RIO, played by STANLEY in his match against ROUSSEAU in 1 845 and by LOWENTHAL against MORPHY in 1 858, became popular after its adoption by Morphy. I n 1 889 STEINITZ wrote, 'on principle this [move] ought to be disadvantageous as it drives the bishop where it wants to go. ' His view has not prevailed. More than a dozen other replies have been tried on Black's third move, but 3 . . . a6 is played more often than all of them put together."
fields.historical_notes: The Oxford Companion names a rival claimant: del Rio. Recorded as disputed rather than resolved.

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Duras Variation'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Duras Variation': "Duras Variation, 2 1 5, a sound line, sometimes called the Moscow Variation, in the QUEEN'S GAMBIT Declined; if 5 Bh4 Black can reply 5 . . . dxc4 or 5 . . . Bb4 + and 6 . . . dxc4, and White cannot respond with Pe2-e4. Another Queen's Gambit line, 1 89, introduced in the game Duras-Balla, Breslau 1 9 1 2. Also 695 and 79 1 , outmoded lines in the SPANISH OPENING, and 687, the KERES VARIATION and 75 1 , the KHOLMOV VARIATION, in the same opening."

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Worrall Attack': "Worrall Attack. 757 in the SPANISH OPENING, first played in the 1 840s. source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Blackmar–Diemer Gambit'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Blackmar–Diemer Gambit': "Blackmar-Diemer Gambit, 55 or 22 1 , a variation of the BLACKMAR GAMBIT. lgnacy Popiel ( 1 863 -1 94 1 ) noted in Deutsches Wochenschach, 1 893, that the Blackmar Gambit (I d4 d5 2 c4 dxe4 3 f3) could be answered effectively by 3 . . . c5; instead of 3 f3 he recommended 3 Nc3, which he called the Polish Gambit in honour of his native land . In 1 932 the German player Emil Josef Diemer ( 1 908 90), following Popicl's analysis, 3 Nc3 Nf6, advocated the continuation 4 f3. The gambit thus modified (which may occur by transposition when the game begins I d4 Nf6) has been played occasionally by gran"
fields.historical_notes: The Oxford Companion names a rival claimant: Popiel. Recorded as disputed rather than resolved.

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Furman Variation'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Furman Variation': "Furman Variation, 69 in the QUEEN'S GAMBIT ACCEPTED. Beginning with 6 Qe2, FURMAN'S plan is to play dxc5 (without allowing a queen exchange on d I ) followed by Pe3-e4-e5."

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Marshall Defense to the Queen's Gambit'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Marshall Defense to the Queen's Gambit': "Marshall Defence, 2 1 9, a dubious variation in the QUEEN'S GAMBIT Declined which MARSHALL tried in the mid- l 920s until the game Alekhine-Marshall, Baden-Baden 1 925, discouraged him."

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Marshall Gambit'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Marshall Gambit': "Marshall Gambit, 1 2 1 and 1 35 in the QUEEN'S GAMBIT Declined. The first was introduced by MARSHALL at Monte Carlo 1904, while the second. a sound way of avoiding the MERAN VARIATION, is as the game Marshall-Schlechter, Monte Carlo 1902. Also 60 1 in the SCANDINAVIAN OPENING, an old line given in the first edition of the HANDBUCH ( 1 843). Marshall played it at Carlsbad 1 907, but it had not fallen out of use; BLACKBURNE was among those who had used it regularly, and it sometimes bears his name."

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Mikenas Variation'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Mikenas Variation': "Mikenas Variation, 285, a sharp attacking line in the MODERN BENONI espoused by MIKENAS from the mid- 1 950s; 1 257 in the ALEKHINE DEFEl'iCE, played in a 1 948 match game Nezhmetdinov-Mikenas. Also 283, the PAWN STORM VARIATION, which may lead to 285."

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Grünfeld Defence'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Grünfeld Defence': "Grunfeld Defence. 363, a popular variation of the KING'S INUIAN DEFENCE named after the grandmaster who introduced it in the fourth game of his match against BECKER, Vienna 1922. In the key variation, 4 cxd5 Nxd5 5 e4 Nxc3 6 bxc3, Black hopes to gain sufficient counterplay by attacking White's CLASSICAL CENTRE (see BLOCKADE; FINE) . Ernst GRUNFELo's idea has been used in other contexts; e.g. the KEMERI, 4 1 6, and COUNTERTHRUST, 4 1 5, VARIATIONS."

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Levenfish Variation'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Levenfish Variation': "Levenfish Variation. 132, a recommendation by LEVENFISH made in the Russian Yearbook, 1 937, in which he gave a 53-page analysis of the QUEEN ' S GAMBIT; 383, line in the GRUNFELD DEFENCE abandoned because of the reply 8 e5; 884, a colourful but possibly unsound sacrifice in the EVANS GAMBIT."

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Flohr Variation'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Flohr Variation': "Flohr Variation, 33 and 44 in the ENGLISH OPENING, the first recommended by ALEKHINE in 1 926 as a refutation of 2 NB, the second introduced by NIMZOWITSCH and taken up successfully by FLOHR in 1 933; 72 in the QUEEN'S GAMBIT ACCEPTED, played by Flohr against RESHEVSKY at Nottingham 1 936 ('seems to rehabilitate the entire line of defence' -Alekhine): 376 and 379 in the GRUNFELD DEFENCE; 466 in the SICILIAN DEFENCE, played by Flohr several times at Nottingham and Moscow in 1 936; 574 in the CARO- KANN DEFENrE, an idea of OPOCENSKY's played twice by Flohr at Moscow 1935: 1 27 1 in the ALEKHINE "

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Makogonov System'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Makogonov System': "Makogonov Variation. 373, a vanat1on in the GRUNFELD DEFENCE introduced by MAKOGONOV in 1 9 5 1 ; 4 1 0 in the KING'S INDIAN DEFENCE."

source_refs: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Sämisch Variation'

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Sämisch Variation': "Sä.misch Variation, 9 J in the SLAV DEFENCE, as Samisch -Alekhine, four-player tournament 1 937; 1 68 in the QUEEN'S GAMBIT Declined, played in the game Samisch Bogoljubow, Budapest 1 92 1 . and popular with ALEKHINE for some years; 299 and 396, standard lines in the NIMZO-INDIAN (see GREEK GIFT; RAGOZIN; SAMISCH) and KING'S INDIAN DEFENCES (see BYRNE; DESPERAU<>; LILIENTHAL; LOMBARDY) respectively, advocated and practised by SAMISCH, perhaps his most important contribution to the game."

fields.attribution_source: Hooper & Whyld, 'The Oxford Companion to Chess' (2nd ed., OUP 1992), entry 'Hübner Variation': "Hubner Variation, 3 1 8 in the NIMZO-INDIAN DEFENCE as Najdorf-Hubner, Wijk aan Zee 1 97 1 . The idea i s to follow with Pd7-d6 and leave White with DOUBLED PAWNS."
